links.why: $\lambda=2\pi/k$ and plane waves: neutron diffraction is the same de Broglie physics as the QM scattering sheets.
Bragg's $2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ and the Laue condition are the same reasoning as spectrometer gratings and X-ray astronomy.

intro: The gate to the Crystal Caverns is a lattice of atoms. Read it in real space (primitive cell, basis, Wigner–Seitz), flip it into reciprocal space (Brillouin zone) and let neutrons tell you which Bragg peaks survive. Every exam so far opened with this.

encounters.title: Lattice, basis and the reciprocal lattice

blocks.html: A crystal is a Bravais lattice $\vec R=n_1\vec a+n_2\vec b+n_3\vec c$ plus a basis: the atoms of one primitive cell, at fractional coordinates $\vec r_j=x_1\vec a+x_2\vec b+x_3\vec c$. A primitive cell contains exactly one lattice point; its volume is $V=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$. The Wigner–Seitz cell (bisectors to all neighbours) is a primitive cell with the full point symmetry.

blocks.tex: \vec a^*=\frac{2\pi}{V}\,\vec b\times\vec c,\quad \vec b^*=\frac{2\pi}{V}\,\vec c\times\vec a,\quad \vec c^*=\frac{2\pi}{V}\,\vec a\times\vec b
blocks.label: (1.4): so a·a* = 2π and a·b* = 0.

blocks.tex: \vec G=h\vec a^*+k\vec b^*+l\vec c^*,\qquad e^{i\vec G\cdot\vec R}=1,\qquad V^*=\frac{(2\pi)^3}{V}
blocks.label: (1.6)-(1.10). 2D: A* = (2π)²/A.

blocks.html: The first Brillouin zone is the Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice. All zones have the same volume $(2\pi)^3/V$. Reciprocal of sc is sc, of bcc is fcc, of fcc is bcc.

$\vec G$ are exactly the wavevectors of plane waves $e^{i\vec G\cdot\vec r}$ that have the periodicity of the lattice. Anything periodic in the crystal (density, potential) is a Fourier sum over $\vec G$ only. Bigger cell in real space means denser reciprocal lattice and smaller Brillouin zone.

Build the reciprocal lattice from the primitive vectors. A centred cell (two lattice points) gives a reciprocal grid with too many points, half of which carry zero intensity. Count lattice points, not atoms: two different atoms in a rectangle = primitive cell with a 2-atom basis; two identical atoms at corner and centre = centred lattice, primitive area $ab/2$.

Every written exam so far (HS23 Jan and Aug, Problem 1) asks in sequence: primitive cell? its area? basis in fractional coordinates? Wigner–Seitz cell and area? reciprocal lattice sketch, first BZ, its area $(2\pi)^2/A$. Then a change of basis (atoms made identical or shifted) and the same again.

encounters.title: Diffraction: where the peaks are and how bright

blocks.html: Scattering from a periodic density gives the amplitude $\sum_{\vec R}e^{i\vec K\cdot\vec R}\,F(\vec K)$ with $\vec K=\vec k_f-\vec k_i$. The lattice sum vanishes unless $\vec K$ is a reciprocal lattice vector:

blocks.tex: I(\vec K)\propto N^2|F(\vec K)|^2\ \text{if}\ \vec K=\vec G,\qquad F(\vec G)=\sum_j f_j\,e^{i\vec G\cdot\vec r_j}=\sum_j f_j\,e^{2\pi i(hx_j+ky_j+lz_j)}
blocks.label: (1.29)-(1.33): Laue condition and structure factor.
(1.34): scattering angle 2θ between k_i and k_f.

blocks.html: The lattice decides where peaks can appear; the basis decides how bright each one is. Identical atoms at special positions cancel some peaks completely (extinction): bcc keeps only $h+k+l$ even, fcc only all-even or all-odd.
$\theta$ versus $2\theta$: the angle between $\vec k_i$ and $\vec k_f$ is $2\theta$. The Zheludev key calls $\theta$ the 'scattering angle'. Write both. And intensities go as $|F|^2$, not $F$.

Ewald construction: a sphere of radius $k$ through the origin of reciprocal space; peaks where it passes through $\vec G$. Rotating a crystal (or using a powder) sweeps it: all $\vec G$ with $|\vec G|\le2k$ are reachable. Debye–Scherrer powder: rings.

HS23: neutrons $\lambda=2.36$ Å, $|\vec k|=2.66$ Å$^{-1}$, angles of the $(2,1)$ and $(1,1)$ peaks, intensity ratio from $F$. HS20: structure factor of BaTiO$_3$, $I(200)/I(110)=9/4$; MC on Laue patterns of sc/fcc/bcc and Debye–Scherrer.

check.q: In a bcc crystal (cubic cell, atoms at $(0,0,0)$ and $(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12)$), which reflection is absent?
Neutrons with $\lambda=2.36$ Å have an energy of about
check.explain: $E=h^2/(2m_n\lambda^2)=81.8/\lambda^2$ meV $=14.7$ meV: the scale of phonons. X-rays of the same $\lambda$ have 5.3 keV.

source.where: Task 1 MC (e),(f),(g),(h),(k); key in solutions/... HS20 (Solution).pdf

questions.q: Which regular polygon can be the unit cell of a 2D crystal lattice (lattice points at its corners)?
questions.explain: Only 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold rotations are compatible with translations. Regular hexagons tile the plane (the hexagon is the Wigner–Seitz cell of the triangular lattice); 5-, 7- and 8-gons cannot.

questions.q: In the Debye–Scherrer method (powder, monochromatic $\lambda_0=2\pi/|\vec k_0|$) one observes, in the Ewald picture,
options: all reflections on a sphere of radius $|\vec k_0|$ about the origin
all reflections on a sphere of radius $|\vec k_0|$ about the point $\vec k_0$
all reflections on a sphere of radius $2|\vec k_0|$ about the origin
all reflections inside a sphere of radius $2|\vec k_0|$ about the origin
questions.explain: Powder = all crystal orientations, so every $\vec G$ with $|\vec G|\le2k_0$ satisfies Laue for some grain.

questions.q: If the volume of a crystal is halved (same material), then
options: the electronic specific heat per volume changes
the number of phonon branches changes
questions.explain: $F$ depends on the basis, $c_V/V$ on the density of states per volume, the branch count on the atoms per cell: all intensive.

questions.q: Laue pattern of an fcc crystal: which reflections survive?
questions.explain: $F=f[1+e^{i\pi(h+k)}+e^{i\pi(h+l)}+e^{i\pi(k+l)}]$ is $4f$ for unmixed and 0 for mixed parity. This is how the HS20 MC (g) patterns distinguish bcc and fcc.

questions.q: The conventional cubic cell of fcc contains how many lattice points?
questions.explain: $8\times\frac18$ corners $+6\times\frac12$ faces $=4$; the primitive cell has volume $a^3/4$.

questions.q: Shifting half of the atoms of a centred rectangular crystal so that the $a\times b$ rectangle becomes the primitive cell makes the first Brillouin zone
questions.explain: Primitive area doubles from $ab/2$ to $ab$, so $A^*=(2\pi)^2/A$ halves (HS23 Aug: 3.95 to 1.97 Å$^{-2}$).

encounters.title: Laue condition is Bragg's law
encounters.goal: Show that the Laue condition $\vec k_f-\vec k_i=\vec G_{hkl}$ for elastic scattering is equivalent to $2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$, where $d$ is the spacing of the lattice planes perpendicular to $\vec G$.
given: $\vec G_{hkl}$ is perpendicular to the planes $(hkl)$ and the shortest such vector has $|\vec G_{hkl}|=2\pi/d_{hkl}$

steps.prompt: Draw $\vec k_i$, $\vec k_f$ and $\vec K=\vec k_f-\vec k_i$ for elastic scattering by an angle $2\theta$. What is $|\vec K|$?
steps.reveal: Isosceles triangle with sides $k,k$ and opening angle $2\theta$: $|\vec K|=2k\sin\theta$, and $\vec K$ bisects the two beams, i.e. the beams make equal angles $\theta$ with the plane perpendicular to $\vec K$ (specular 'reflection').

steps.prompt: Why must the planes be perpendicular to $\vec G$ for the picture to work?
steps.reveal: $e^{i\vec G\cdot\vec r}$ is constant on planes $\vec G\cdot\vec r=$ const spaced by $2\pi/|\vec G|$: those are the lattice planes; reflection from them is the grating picture of Fig. 1.8.

steps.prompt: Apply: HS23 Aug, $\lambda=2.36$ Å, $(2,1)$ of a $4\times5$ Å rectangle. $d$ and $\theta$?

keyPoints: $|\vec K|=2k\sin\theta$ from the elastic triangle
$|\vec G|=2\pi n/d$ with $\vec G\perp$ planes
$2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$
scattering angle is $2\theta$

encounters.title: The two-atom rectangular crystal (neutrons at the gate)
encounters.problem: Zheludev, Jan 2024, Problem 1 (2D crystal). Rectangular lattice, $a=6.0$ Å along $x$ and $b=4.0$ Å along $y$. Filled circles (scattering amplitude $f_1$) sit at the lattice points $(0,0)$; empty circles ($f_2$) sit at the cell centre, fractional coordinates $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$. So the primitive cell is the rectangle spanned by $\vec a,\vec b$ and the basis has two atoms. Neutrons of wavelength $\lambda=2.36$ Å scatter elastically. Peaks are labelled $\vec q=h\vec a^*+k\vec b^*$ with $|\vec a^*|=2\pi/a$, $|\vec b^*|=2\pi/b$.

steps.prompt: Area of the primitive cell $A=ab$, in Å$^2$.
steps.hint: Rectangle spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$. It contains one lattice point and two atoms, so it is primitive.

steps.prompt: Area of the first Brillouin zone $(2\pi)^2/A$, in Å$^{-2}$.
steps.hint: The BZ is the Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice, which is again a rectangle: $(2\pi/a)(2\pi/b)=(2\pi)^2/A$ (script 1.3).

steps.prompt: Magnitude of the incident wavevector $|\vec k_i|=|\vec k_f|=2\pi/\lambda$, in Å$^{-1}$.
steps.hint: Elastic scattering: $|\vec k_f|=|\vec k_i|$. The key prints 2.66 Å$^{-1}$.

steps.prompt: Bragg angle $\theta$ for the $(2,1)$ peak in degrees, from $Q=4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda$ with $Q=2\pi\sqrt{(h/a)^2+(k/b)^2}$. ($2\theta$ is the angle between $\vec k_i$ and $\vec k_f$.)
steps.hint: $\sin\theta=\frac{\lambda}{2}\sqrt{(h/a)^2+(k/b)^2}=\lambda|\vec G|/4\pi$. Laue: $\vec k_f-\vec k_i=\vec G$ and $|\vec G|=2k\sin\theta$.

steps.prompt: Bragg angle $\theta$ for the $(1,1)$ peak, in degrees.
steps.hint: Same formula with $h=k=1$ (key: $\theta=20.7^\circ$, i.e. $2\theta=41.5^\circ$ between the beams).
$h+k=3$ gives $F=f_1-f_2$; $h+k=2$ gives $F=f_1+f_2$. Intensity $I\propto|F|^2$, so $(1/3)^2=1/9$. For $f_1=f_2$ the $(2,1)$ peak is extinct (the lattice would then be centred).

steps.prompt: (Bonus) The angle between $\vec k_i$ and $\vec k_f$ for the $(2,1)$ peak, i.e. $2\theta$, in degrees.
steps.hint: The exam key prints $\theta=29.5^\circ$ and calls it the scattering angle. Strictly the angle between $\vec k_i$ and $\vec k_f$ is $2\theta$: say which one you give.

encounters.title: Shift the atoms: the unit cell doubles
encounters.problem: Zheludev, Aug 2024, Problem 1. A rectangular crystal of identical atoms, $\vec a=(0,4)$ Å, $\vec b=(5,0)$ Å, with atoms at the corners and, in the first configuration, at the cell centre $\vec d=\frac12(\vec a+\vec b)$. In the second configuration the centre atoms are shifted to $\vec d=\frac13(\vec a+\vec b)$ while $\vec a,\vec b$ stay unchanged. Neutrons $\lambda=2.36$ Å. Peaks $(h,k)=h\vec a^*+k\vec b^*$.

steps.prompt: First configuration (atom at the centre): area of the primitive cell in Å$^2$.
steps.hint: The cell $\vec a,\vec b$ is not primitive now: it holds two identical atoms. A primitive cell has area $ab/2$ (e.g. spanned by $(\vec a+\vec b)/2$ and $(\vec a-\vec b)/2$).

steps.prompt: Area of the first Brillouin zone of the first configuration, Å$^{-2}$.
steps.hint: $(2\pi)^2/A_1=3.95$ Å$^{-2}$. The BZ is twice as large as for the $a\times b$ rectangle.

steps.prompt: Second configuration ($\vec d=\frac13(\vec a+\vec b)$): now $\vec a,\vec b$ is primitive with a two-atom basis at $(0,0)$ and $(\frac13,\frac13)$. Area of the first BZ in Å$^{-2}$.
steps.hint: $A_2=ab=20$ Å$^2$, so $A^*=(2\pi)^2/20=1.97$ Å$^{-2}$. Shifting the atoms halves the BZ again.

steps.prompt: Bragg angle of the $(2,1)$ peak, in degrees. Here $|\vec a^*|=2\pi/4$ Å$^{-1}$ along the short axis, $|\vec b^*|=2\pi/5$ Å$^{-1}$.
Bragg angle of the $(1,1)$ peak, in degrees.

encounters.title: How many spots can the detector ever see?
encounters.problem: Fermi estimate (quick fight, within a factor of 1.3). Powder or single crystal: Bragg reflection requires $|\vec G|\le 2k=4\pi/\lambda$ (the Ewald sphere never reaches farther). A simple cubic crystal with $a=5$ Å is probed with Cu K$\alpha$, $\lambda=1.54$ Å. Estimate the number $N$ of reciprocal lattice points inside the sphere $|\vec G|\le 2k$ (the origin included).

steps.prompt: $N$ = (volume of the sphere)/(volume per reciprocal lattice point $(2\pi/a)^3$).
(Bonus) The same crystal but bcc with cubic cell $a$ (reflections with $h+k+l$ even only): how many of these points are allowed?
steps.hint: For bcc the structure factor is $f(1+e^{i\pi(h+k+l)})$: half of all points are extinct. For fcc only $h,k,l$ all even or all odd survive: one quarter.

encounters.title: Boss: BaTiO$_3$, the perovskite (exam problem)

source.where: Task 2 'Kristallstruktur von BaTiO3' (14 pt, Ensslin practice exam HS20); solution: materials/solid-state/solutions/Einführung in die Festkörperphysik HS20 (Solution).pdf

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (translated from the German exam). Then enter the numerical final answers; the derivation parts are self-graded against the key points.
statement: Barium titanate $\mathrm{BaTiO_3}$ crystallises in the (barium-)perovskite structure: a Ba atom sits on each corner of a cube, a Ti atom in the cube centre and an O atom in the centre of each face. Cube edge $a$; origin at a Ba corner, as in the figure.
(a) [2 pt] Which Bravais lattice? Give the basis vectors $\vec a_i$.
(b) [2 pt] Give the basis (positions and species) within a primitive cell. How many atoms of each element does the primitive cell contain?
(c) [2 pt] Give the reciprocal basis $\vec g_i$ belonging to the $\vec a_i$ of (a). Which Bravais lattice is the reciprocal lattice?
(d) [2 pt] What shape is the first Brillouin zone? What is the volume of the third Brillouin zone?

(e) [4 pt] Bragg scattering from BaTiO$_3$: determine the structure factor $S(\vec G)$ for arbitrary $\vec G$ and evaluate it for the (110) plane. Take $f_{\rm Ba}=5f_{\rm O}$, $f_{\rm Ti}=4f_{\rm O}$ and $f_{\rm O}(\vec G)=f_{\rm O}$.
(f) [2 pt] Compute the ratio of the Bragg intensities of the (200) and (110) planes.
Game numbers: $a=4.00$ Å (close to the real $a=4.01$ Å) and Cu K$\alpha$, $\lambda=1.5406$ Å.

finalAnswers.prompt: (b) Atoms in the primitive cell (all species together).
(e) $S(110)$ in units of $f_{\rm O}$ (real part; for integer $h,k,l$ the phases are $\pm1$).
(f) $S(200)$ in units of $f_{\rm O}$.
(d) Volume of any Brillouin zone $(2\pi/a)^3$ in Å$^{-3}$.
Extra: Bragg angle $\theta$ of the (110) reflection for Cu K$\alpha$ in degrees ($d_{110}=a/\sqrt2$).

keyPoints: (a) Simple cubic Bravais lattice, $\vec a_1=(a,0,0)$, $\vec a_2=(0,a,0)$, $\vec a_3=(0,0,a)$: the corner, centre and face-centre positions are not lattice translations of each other.
(b) Basis: Ba $(0,0,0)$; Ti $(\frac a2,\frac a2,\frac a2)$; O $(\frac a2,\frac a2,0)$, $(\frac a2,0,\frac a2)$, $(0,\frac a2,\frac a2)$. Five atoms: 1 Ba, 1 Ti, 3 O.
(c) $\vec g_i\cdot\vec a_j=2\pi\delta_{ij}$ gives $\vec g_i=(2\pi/a)\hat e_i$: again simple cubic, with edge $2\pi/a$.
(d) First BZ is a cube of edge $2\pi/a$; every BZ has the same volume $(2\pi/a)^3$.

(e) $S(\vec G)=\sum_\alpha f_\alpha e^{i\vec G\cdot\vec r_\alpha}=f_{\rm Ba}+f_{\rm Ti}e^{i\pi(h+k+l)}+f_{\rm O}\big(e^{i\pi(h+k)}+e^{i\pi(h+l)}+e^{i\pi(k+l)}\big)$, with $\vec G=\frac{2\pi}{a}(h,k,l)$. For (110): $5+4+1-1-1=8f_{\rm O}$.
Intensity $I\propto|S|^2$ (kinematic approximation, script 1.5).

encounters.title: Boss: two-dimensional crystals, January 2024 (exam problem)

source.where: Problem 1 'Two-dimensional crystals' (3 pt, Zheludev, 25 Jan 2024, parts a-r); solution: materials/solid-state/solutions/Einführung in die Festkörperphysik HS23 (Solution) (1).pdf, Solution 1

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (the exam gives 3 pt for the whole problem; the key counts each of the 18 parts 1/6 pt). Sketches are self-graded against the key points; enter the numbers below.
statement: Two-dimensional crystal. Figure: a rectangular array; filled circles at the corners of the rectangle, a blue arrow $\vec b$ pointing up (length $b=4.0$ Å) and $\vec a$ pointing right (length $a=6.0$ Å) with a right-angle mark at the origin; one empty circle sits in the middle of every $a\times b$ rectangle, i.e. at the centre of the rectangle spanned by $\vec a,\vec b$. Empty and filled circles are two different atoms.
(a) Is the parallelogram spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ a primitive unit cell?
(b) What is the area $A$ of the primitive unit cell?
(c) What is the basis of this crystal? Write down the coordinates of the atomic positions for each atom within the basis in the unit cell spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.
(d) Sketch a Wigner–Seitz unit cell. What is its area?

In two dimensions the reciprocal basis is $\vec a^*=\frac{2\pi}{A}(\vec b\times\hat z)$, $\vec b^*=\frac{2\pi}{A}(\hat z\times\vec a)$, with $A$ the area of the primitive cell and $\hat z=\hat a\times\hat b$.
(e) Sketch the reciprocal lattice of the crystal.   (f) Draw the first Brillouin zone in your sketch.   (g) What is the area of the first Brillouin zone?

Neutron diffraction with monochromatic neutrons of wavelength $\lambda=2.36$ Å. The scattering density is $\rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_i f_i\,\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)$, $\mathbf r_i$ the nucleus position of the $i$-th atom in the unit cell and $f_i$ the amplitude of its scattering potential. The values of $f_i$ of the atoms represented by the empty and the filled circles are $f_1$ and $f_2$, respectively.
(h) Assuming elastic scattering, what are the magnitudes of the wavevectors $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ of the incident and reflected beams?
(i) Calculate the scattering angle between $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ for the two Bragg peaks $\mathbf q=(2,1)$ and $(1,1)$, where $\mathbf q=(h,k)=h\vec a^*+k\vec b^*$.
(j) Compare the intensities $I$ of the two peaks. Calculate $I_{(2,1)}/I_{(1,1)}$ if $f_1=2f_2$.
(k) Calculate the intensities of the two peaks if all atoms are identical, $f_1=f_2$.
From now on all atoms are identical. Figure: the same crystal with all circles filled (the centre atoms drawn as filled dots), vectors $\vec a,\vec b$ as before.

(l) Is the parallelogram spanned by $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ a primitive unit cell?   (m) Sketch a primitive cell. What is its area $A_1$?   (n) What is the basis? Give the coordinates of the atoms in the primitive cell you sketched.   (o) Sketch a Wigner–Seitz cell. What is its area?   (p) Sketch the reciprocal lattice.   (q) Draw the first Brillouin zone.   (r) What is the area of the first Brillouin zone?
Note on the key: it quotes the Bragg angle $\theta$ (from $Q=4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda$) for part (i); the angle between $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ is $2\theta$. Give both below.

finalAnswers.prompt: (b) Area $A$ of the primitive cell in Å$^2$.
(d) Area of the Wigner–Seitz cell in Å$^2$.
(g) Area of the first Brillouin zone in Å$^{-2}$.
(h) $|\mathbf k_i|=|\mathbf k_f|$ in Å$^{-1}$.
(i) Bragg angle $\theta$ of the $(2,1)$ peak in degrees (key: 29.47$^\circ$).
(i) Bragg angle $\theta$ of the $(1,1)$ peak in degrees (key: 20.73$^\circ$; exact 20.77$^\circ$).
(i) Full scattering angle $2\theta$ between $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ for $(2,1)$, in degrees.
(k) Identical atoms: $I_{(1,1)}$ in units of $f_1^2$ (the $(2,1)$ peak has $I=0$, extinct).
(m) Area $A_1$ of the primitive cell of the identical-atom crystal in Å$^2$.
(r) Area of the first Brillouin zone of the identical-atom crystal in Å$^{-2}$.

keyPoints: (a) Yes: the rectangle contains exactly one lattice point (four corners times 1/4); the lattice is primitive rectangular.

(b), (d) $A=ab=24$ Å$^2$. The Wigner–Seitz cell of a rectangular lattice is the rectangle $a\times b$ centred on a lattice point (perpendicular bisectors of the nearest neighbours), also area 24 Å$^2$.
(c) Two atoms: $\mathbf r_1=(0,0)$ (filled) and $\mathbf r_2=(\frac12,\frac12)$ (empty), in fractional coordinates of $\vec a,\vec b$.
(e)-(g) $\vec a^*\parallel\vec a$, $|\vec a^*|=2\pi/a$, $|\vec b^*|=2\pi/b$: rectangular lattice. The first BZ is the rectangle $|q_x|\le\pi/a$, $|q_y|\le\pi/b$, area $(2\pi)^2/(ab)=1.64$ Å$^{-2}$.
(h) $k=2\pi/\lambda=2.66$ Å$^{-1}$ for both (elastic).

(i) $Q=4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda$ with $|\mathbf q|=2\pi\sqrt{(h/a)^2+(k/b)^2}$: $\theta_{(2,1)}=\arcsin[\frac\lambda2\sqrt{(2/a)^2+(1/b)^2}]=29.5^\circ$ (key 29.47$^\circ$), $\theta_{(1,1)}=20.8^\circ$ (key 20.73$^\circ$); angle between $\mathbf k_i,\mathbf k_f$ is $2\theta=58.9^\circ$ and $41.5^\circ$.
(l) No: the $a\times b$ rectangle now contains two lattice points (centred rectangular lattice).

(m)-(o) Primitive cell e.g. spanned by $\frac12(\vec a+\vec b)$ and $\frac12(\vec a-\vec b)$ (or $\vec a$ and $\frac12(\vec a+\vec b)$), area $A_1=ab/2=12$ Å$^2$; basis one atom at $(0,0)$ of that cell; the Wigner–Seitz cell is a hexagon-like cell of the same area 12 Å$^2$ (the key sketches it).
(p)-(r) The reciprocal lattice is also centred rectangular (the $h+k$ odd points of the old lattice are missing), first BZ area $(2\pi)^2/A_1=3.29$ Å$^{-2}$ $=8\pi^2/(ab)$: twice the earlier one.
Printed key remark: in (d) the key calls the given rectangle a Wigner–Seitz cell with $A=24$ Å$^2$.

encounters.title: Boss: two-dimensional crystals, August 2024 (exam problem)

source.where: Problem 1 'Two-dimensional crystals' (3 pt, Zheludev, 16 Aug 2024, parts a-o); solution: materials/solid-state/solutions/Einführung in die Festkörperphysik HS23 (Solution).pdf, Solution 1 (0.2 pt per correct part)

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (3 pt total, 0.2 pt per part in the key). Sketches are self-graded against the key points; enter the numbers below.
statement: Two-dimensional crystal. Figure: a rectangular array of identical atoms (all circles are the same atom). The arrows are $\vec a=(0,4)$ Å (pointing up) and $\vec b=(5,0)$ Å (pointing right) from a corner atom, and $\vec d=\frac12(\vec a+\vec b)$ (pointing to the middle of the rectangle). There is an extra atom in the middle of every $a\times b$ rectangle (at $\vec d$ from each corner atom): the array is a centred rectangular lattice.
(a) For this lattice write down two vectors that define a primitive unit cell.
(b) What is the basis of this crystal? Give the coordinates of the atomic positions for each atom within the basis in the unit cell of (a).
(c) Sketch a Wigner–Seitz cell. What is its area?

Reciprocal vectors in 2D: $\vec a^*=\frac{2\pi}{A}(\vec b\times\hat z)$, $\vec b^*=\frac{2\pi}{A}(\hat z\times\vec a)$, with $A$ the area of the primitive cell in real space and $\hat z=\hat a\times\hat b$.
(d) Sketch the reciprocal lattice.   (e) Draw the first Brillouin zone.   (f) What is the area of the first Brillouin zone?

Second configuration. Figure: the same $a\times b$ array, but now half of the atoms are shifted: the atoms in the middle of the rectangles move (red arrows, towards the lower left) so that they sit at $\vec d=\frac13(\vec a+\vec b)$ from the corner atoms; $\vec a,\vec b$ unchanged.
(g) For this lattice write down two vectors that define a primitive unit cell.
(h) What is the basis? Give the coordinates of the atoms in the unit cell of (g).
(i) Sketch a Wigner–Seitz cell and give its area.   (j) Sketch the reciprocal lattice.   (k) Draw the first Brillouin zone.   (l) What is the area of the first Brillouin zone?

Neutron diffraction with monochromatic neutrons of wavelength $\lambda=2.36$ Å. The scattering density is $\rho(\mathbf r)=\sum_i f_i\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_i)$ with $\mathbf r_i$ the nucleus position of the $i$-th atom in the crystal; all atoms have $f_i=f_1$.
(m) Assuming elastic scattering, what are the magnitudes of $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$?
(n) Calculate the scattering angle between $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ for the Bragg peaks $\mathbf q=(2,1)$ and $(1,1)$, $\mathbf q=(h,k)=h\vec a^*+k\vec b^*$ (second configuration).
(o) Compare the intensities of the two peaks. Calculate $I_{(2,1)}/I_{(1,1)}$.
